# Efficiency for RAL Estimators

In @sec-3-AL we defined *asymptotic linearity* (AL) and discussed why AL estimators are nice: they are asymptotically unbiased, are easy to do inference for, and can be (asymptotically) compared by looking at their influence functions. In @sec-3-regularity we argued that we should further restrict the class of desirable estimators to those that are *regular* so that bad finite-sample behavior can't be hidden in the asymptotic comparisons. In this chapter we will establish the central result of efficiency theory: in any model where the estimand varies smoothly enough over the different distributions, there is a best-possible regular asymptotically linear (RAL) estimator.

Really what we'll prove is that there is a best-possible *influence function*: multiple estimators may have that influence function but by virtue of that fact they will behave similarly in large-enough samples. We call the best-possible influence function the *efficient* influence function (EIF). The EIF sets a limit on how good any RAL estimator can be at estimating some estimand in a some model. If you have a RAL estimator with that influence function, you can rest assured that it is the best you can do (asymptotically).

In this chapter we will prove our central result and discuss some important implications. In the next chapter we'll show how to derive the EIF in the most common scenarios. After that, in the last part of the book, we will demonstrate how to use knowledge of the EIF to *construct* efficient estimators.

## Characterizing Influence Functions

Not every possible function corresponds to a valid RAL estimator of an estimand in a particular statistical model. Clearly it would be wonderful if we could find a RAL estimator with $\phi(z) = 0$ because this estimator would have no variance at all in large samples. But if that were possible, statistics would be easy. So $\phi(z) = 0$ must not be an influence function for any sensible estimand in any sensible model. So, for a given estimand and statistical model, what functions are influence functions of RAL estimators, and what functions aren't?

We already know that any regular estimator by definition behaves in a particular way asymptotically along a quickly-converging sequence of distributions. Remarkably, it turns out that asymptotic linearity also implies specific asymptotic behavior along a subset of these sequences.

:::: callout-note
# Asymptotic linearity along differentiable paths

::: {#thm-LAN}
Let $\model_\eps \subseteq \model$ be any differentiable path with score function $s$ and let $\p^{(\eps_n)}$ be a sequence of distributions along this path with $\eps_n = c_n n^{-1/2}$ for any converging sequence of real numbers $c_n \to c$ . Let $\p = \p^{(0)}$ denote the true data-generating distribution.

If an estimator $\hat\Psi$ is asymptotically linear with influence function $\phi$, then

$$
\sqrt{n}\left( \hat\Psi(\p^{(\eps_n)}_n) - \Psi(\p) \right) \rightsquigarrow \norm(\p[s\phi], \p \phi^2)
.
$$
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
# Proof Outline

A thorough proof of this result is too technical for this book so I will only give an outline here. While I do encourage you to dig into the theory if you are curious (since it has other applications as well), I think this is best done *after* understanding the implications of the result in our present context.

Let $p$ and $p_{\eps_n}$ denote the densities of $\p = \p^{(0)}$ and $\p^{(\eps_n)}$, respectively (you can either assume we're working in a model with densities or recall that we can always construct densities along sequences of a differentiable path).

The first step is to show that any differentiable path is in fact a *locally asymptotically normal* (LAN) model. This is proved as Theorem 7.2 in @vdv and while the arguments are accessible with basic asymptotic statistics, I don't think they add too much insight. In LAN models we only consider sequences of the type $\eps_n = c_n n^{-1/2}$ where $c_n \to 1$. This kind of sequence is a special case of the sequences where $\sqrt n \eps_n$ stays bounded that we considered in the definition of regularity. The reason we need to consider this special case is that these are the sequences for which $\sqrt n( \sqrt{p_{\eps_n}} - \sqrt{p} )$ converges in $\eltwo$ to a fixed limit $\frac{1}{2}s \sqrt{p}$ (by @def-score). The $\sqrt n$ convergence of the root densities is required to show that

$$
\sum_i^n \log \frac{p_{\eps_n}(Z_i)}{p(Z_i)}
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum^n s(Z_i)
- \frac{1}{2} \E[s(Z)^2] + \op(1)
$$

along such sequences. When the above holds for a model along such sequences, we say the model is LAN.

The LAN property has nothing to do with any estimator, it is purely a statement about what the densities of nearby distributions $p_{\eps_n}$ look like relative to $p$ as we sample more data from them and move closer to $p$. The log density ratio shown above is actually exactly of the form you get if you instead look at the log density ratio of two normal distributions with the same variance but different means. That's why the property is called local asymptotic normality. So the result says that as you "zoom in" to a point on a differentiable path while sampling more data, the model looks more and more like a set of normal distributions with different means. This happens for any path where the densities vary smoothly (differentiably).

Incredibly, local asymptotic normality tells us enough about what the densities of nearby data-generating distributions look like to infer how any asymptotically linear estimator behaves along these sequences of distributions. The implied pathwise behavior is

$$
\sqrt{n}\left( \hat\Psi(\p^{(\eps_n)}_n) - \Psi(\p) \right) \rightsquigarrow \norm(\p[s\phi], \p \phi^2)
$$

as desired. The technical mechanism for inferring this is called Le Cam's 3rd Lemma (see Example 6.7 in @vdv). To prove the result in generality requires contiguity arguments (Chapter 6 of @vdv), but if you assume that every distribution in the model has a density and that all the densities have the same support (set of values $z$ for which the density is nonzero), then you can prove an equivalent result using only "basic" arguments (continuous mapping and a characteristic function argument). Either way, I don't think the proof gives much intuition that's relevant to our purposes so I've omitted it.
:::

This is remarkable because asymptotic linearity is a pointwise property: it describes only what happens if the estimator is evaluated with more and more data sampled from the *same* distribution. By itself it says nothing about what would happen if we also *changed* that distribution while letting $n$ grow. But if we take into account differentiability along the path suddenly we can understand that changing pathwise behavior. Moreover the pathwise behavior depends crucially on what the score $s$ is for the path in question: notice that the mean of the limiting distribution is $\p s\phi$.

The benefit of knowing this is that now we can compare to the definition of regularity (@def-regularity-pathwise), which *also* tells us how the estimator behaves along sequences including the kind we considered in @thm-LAN, but this time in a way that does *not* depend on what the score is for the path:

$$
\sqrt{n}\left( \hat\Psi(\p^{(\eps_n)}_n) - \Psi(\p^{(\eps_n)}) \right) \rightsquigarrow \mathbb D
.
$$

Recall that $\mathbb D$ is some fixed distribution that by definition is not allowed to depend on the sequence or path. If we let $\eps_n = 0$ (a valid choice), the resulting sequence is $\sqrt{n}\left( \hat\Psi(\p_n) - \Psi(\p) \right)$ which converges to $\norm(0,\p \phi^2)$ when the estimator is asymptotically normal (@def-AL). Since the limiting distribution $\mathbb D$ must be the same across all paths for the estimator to be regular at $\p$, it must be that $\mathbb D = \norm(0,\p \phi^2)$.

Therefore, combining this and @thm-LAN, for any estimator that is both regular *and* asymptotically linear,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{n}\left( \hat\Psi(\p^{(\eps_n)}_n) - \Psi(\p) \right) &\rightsquigarrow \norm(\p[s\phi], \p \phi^2) \\
\sqrt{n}\left( \hat\Psi(\p^{(\eps_n)}_n) - \Psi(\p^{(\eps_n)}) \right) &\rightsquigarrow \norm(0,\p \phi^2)
\end{aligned}
$$

for any sequences $\p^{(\eps_n)}$ along a differentiable path with $\eps_n = c_n n^{-1/2}$ and $c_n \to 1$. Comparing the left- and right-hand sides above, the only way that both asymptotic statements can be true simultaneously is if

$$
\sqrt n \left( \Psi(\p^{(\eps_n)}) - \Psi(\p) \right) \to \p[s\phi].
$$

Because $\eps_n \sim 1/\sqrt n$ and the choice of differentiable path was arbitrary, this implies the following result.

:::: callout-note
# Influence Functions of RAL Estimators

::: {#thm-RAL-IFs}
If $\phi$ is an influence function of an estimator that is RAL at $\p \in \mathcal P$, then

$$
\lim_{\eps \to 0} \frac{\Psi(\p^{(\eps)}) - \Psi(\p^{(0)})}{\eps} = \p s\phi
$$

for any differentiable path $\model_\eps = \{\p^{(\eps)}: \eps \in \reals\}$ with score function $s$.

We often abbreviate the left-hand side of the above with the notation $\dot\Psi(s)$ to indicate that it is a derivative of $\Psi$ at $\p$ in the "direction" $s$ in which case the identity is written cleanly as

$$
\dot\Psi_{\p}(s) = \p s\phi.
$$

Any asymptotically linear estimator with influence function $\phi$ that satisfies this identity for all differentiable paths is regular at $\p \in \model$.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
# Proof

At first it may seem like there is nothing to prove since substituting $\sqrt n \approx \eps_n^{-1}$ appears to do the trick, but just because

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{f(\eps_n) - f(0)}{\eps_n} = \dot f
$$

for all sequences $\eps_n = c_n n^{-1/2}$ with $c_n \to 1$ does not obviously imply that the same is true for *any* sequence $\eps_n \to 0$ (here I am abbreviating $f(\eps) = \Psi(\p^{(\eps)})$ and $\dot f = \p s\phi$). The latter convergence along any sequence $\eps_n \to 0$ is what we need for the left-hand side above to define a derivative.

To do this rigorously requires a little more effort. The rigorous proof is a bit tedious and not at all important to understand if you are happy to believe the result. I include it here only because it relies only on standard tools from analysis and I have not found a thorough version elsewhere in the literature.

In terms of the abbreviations with $f$, the display above @thm-RAL-IFs says that

$$
\sqrt n [f(\eps_n) - f(0)] \to \dot f.
$$

Since $\eps_n = c_n n^{-1/2}$, the above is equivalent to

$$
c_n \eps_n^{-1} [f(\eps_n) - f(0)] \to \dot f.
$$

Since $c_n \to 1$ this happens only if $\eps_n^{-1} [f(\eps_n) - f(0)] \to \dot f$. Therefore $\eps_n^{-1} [f(\eps_n) - f(0)] \to \dot f$ for all $\eps_n - c_n n^{-1/2}$ with $c_n \to 1$. However to prove the theorem we need this to hold for all $\eps_n \to 0$. To show this, we start by picking any sequence $\eta_m \to 0$. Our goal is be to show that this can be written in a way similar to $c_n n^{-1/2}$ with $c_n\to 1$ so that the difference quotient $\eta_n^{-1} [f(\eta_n) - f(0)]$ converges for this sequence by what we've already shown.

Let $n_m = \lfloor 1/\eta_m^2 \rfloor$ be the value of $1/\eta_m^2 \ge 0$ rounded down to the nearest integer for each $m$. Since $\eta_m \to 0$ by assumption, $n_m$ is a sequence of positive integers that is eventually diverging. If we define $c_m = \eta_m n_m = \eta_m \sqrt{\left\lfloor 1/\eta_m^2 \right\rfloor}$ then $|c_m| \to 1$ because the function $\sqrt{\lfloor 1/\eta^2 \rfloor}$ gets closer and closer to $\sqrt{1/\eta^2 }$ as $\eta$ gets smaller.

If you care to see that rigorously, let $\zeta = 1/\eta^2$, which must diverge. The desired convergence

$$
\left| \sqrt{1/\eta^2 } - \sqrt{\lfloor 1/\eta^2 \rfloor}  \right|\overset{\eta \to 0}\to 0
$$

is true if

$$
\left| \sqrt{ \zeta } - \sqrt{\lfloor \zeta \rfloor} \right| \overset{\zeta \to \infty}\to 0.
$$

but

$$
\left| \sqrt{ \zeta } - \sqrt{\lfloor \zeta \rfloor} \right| 
= 
\sqrt{ \zeta } - \sqrt{\lfloor \zeta \rfloor}
\le
\sqrt{ \lfloor\zeta\rfloor +1 } - \sqrt{\lfloor \zeta \rfloor}
= 
\frac{1}{\sqrt{ \lfloor\zeta\rfloor +1 } + \sqrt{\lfloor \zeta \rfloor}}
$$

The final expression on the right converges to zero for any $\zeta \to \infty$, which establishes $|c_m| \to 1$.

We have therefore established that any sequence $\eta_m \to 0$ can be represented as a sequence $c_m / \sqrt{n_m}$ where $|c_m| \to 1$ and $n_m$ are integers diverging to infinity. This is almost of the form we need except for the fact that 1) $n_m$ is an arbitrary diverging sequence of integers rather than the counting sequence $\{1,2,3 \dots \}$ and 2) we have $|c_m| \to 1$ instead of $c_m \to 1$. To resolve this we will first assume $c_m \to 1$ and show that the convergence of the difference quotient along sequences $c_n / \sqrt{n}$ actually implies convergence along sequences $c_{m} / \sqrt{n_m}$ first with $n_m$ strictly increasing and then with $n_m$ an arbitrary diverging sequence of integers. After that is done we will address the issue of the absolute value on $c_m$.

For any increasing sequence $n_m$ and sequence $c_{m} \to 1$, build the "supersequence" $\tilde c_n = c_m$ for all $n_m \le n < n_{m+1}$ so that $c_m = \tilde c_{n_m}$ by construction and $\tilde c_{n} \to 1$ since $c_m \to 1$. Again by construction, $\tilde\eta_m =  \tilde c_{n_m}/\sqrt {n_m}$ is a subsequence of $\eps_n = c_n / \sqrt{n}$ which is of the desired form. Because of that, $\tilde\eta_m^{-1} [f(\tilde\eta_m) - f(0)]$ is a subsequence of $\eps_n^{-1} [f(\eps_n) - f(0)]$ and thus must converge to the same limit $\dot f$.

Now let $n_m$ be an arbitrary, diverging, positive sequence of integers and $c_m \to 1$. Since $n_m$ is diverging, any subsequence $n_{m_k}$ is also diverging. From any diverging subsequence we can take a strictly increasing subsequence $n_{m_{k_j}} < n_{m_{k_{j+1}}}$. Along this sub-subsequence, $c_{m_{k_j}} \to 1$. Therefore, letting $\bar\eta_j = c_{m_{k_j}} / \sqrt{n_{m_{k_j}}}$, we know that $\bar\eta_j^{-1} [f(\bar\eta_j) - f(0)] \to \dot f$ because $\bar\eta_j$ satisfies the conditions required from the paragraph above. Since every subsequence $\left( \frac{c_{m_k}}{\sqrt{n_{m_k}}} \right)^{-1} \left[f\left( \frac{c_{m_k}}{\sqrt{n_{m_k}}} \right) - f(0)\right]$ has a further subsequence that converges to a common limit $\dot f$, that means the original sequence $\left( \frac{c_{m}}{\sqrt{n_{m}}} \right)^{-1} \left[f\left( \frac{c_{m}}{\sqrt{n_{m}}} \right) - f(0)\right]$ also converges to that common limit. This is a consequence of the fact that a sequence converges if and only if all of its subsequences converge to the same limit.

Now we deal with the issue of the absolute value on the sequence $c_m$. To do this we consider a sequence along a path $\model_\eps$ indexed by $\eps_n = c_n n^{-1/2}$ with $c_n \to -1$ instead of $c_n \to 1$. This is exactly the same as a sequence with $c_n \to 1$ but along the "reversed" path $\model_{-\eps}$ which has score $-s$ (see @exr-scaled-score). Therefore along such sequences $c_n \eps_n^{-1}[f(\eps_n) - f(0)] \to -\dot f$ by our starting proposition. Multiplying both sides by $-1$ we obtain that $(-c_n) \eps_n^{-1}[f(\eps_n) - f(0)] \to \dot f$ for any sequence $c_n \to -1$ and $\eps_n = c_n n^{-1/2}$. Since $-c_n \to 1$, by the argument at the beginning of this proof we know that $\eps_n^{-1}[f(\eps_n) - f(0)] \to \dot f$ for any sequence $\eps_n = c_n n^{-1/2}$ now for either $c_n \to 1$ *or* $c_n \to -1$.

We may now return to our original sequence $c_m = \eta_m n_m$ whose absolute value converges to 1. In a mild abuse of notation let $c_m^+$ be the subsequence of the non-negative entries of $c_m$ and let $c_m^-$ be the negative entries (with corresponding subsequences $n_m^+$ and $n_m^-$ which are both diverging sequences of integers). If $c_m^+$ has a finite number of elements then $c_m \to -1$ and otherwise if $c_m^-$ has a finite number of elements then $c_m \to 1$. Either way $\eta_m^{-1}[f(\eta_m) - f(0)] \to \dot f$ by the argument of the paragraph above. In the case that both $c_m^+$ and $c_m^-$ are infinite sequences, $|c_m| \to 1$ implies that $c_m^+ \to 1$ and $c_m^- \to -1$. Therefore we may divide $eta_m$ into the two corresponding sequences $\eta_m^+$ and $\eta_m^-$ and since $(\eta_m^{\pm})^{-1}[f(\eta_m^{\pm}) - f(0)] \to \dot f$ for either part of the sequence it must be that $\eta_m^{-1}[f(\eta_m) - f(0)] \to \dot f$ for the entire sequence.

Lastly, the claim that any asymptotically linear estimator with influence function $\phi$ that satisfies $\dot\Psi_\p(s)=\p s\phi$ for all differentiable paths is automatically regular at $\p \in \model$ comes from running the argument above in reverse: if the conclusion holds and asymptotic linearity holds, then regularity must hold or else a contradiction arises (see also Proposition 1 in Chapter 3 or @bkrw).
:::

This is an astounding result because it connects two seemingly unrelated things: the left-hand side is the rate of change in the estimand as we move the underlying distribution along a path. That has nothing to do with any estimator. The right-hand side is some measure of the "angle" between the influence function of an estimator and the direction of the path. By assuming regularity and asymptotic normality we have managed to connect these two seemingly unrelated quantities. What this means about the set of possible influence functions may still be unclear, but for the moment I hope you can appreciate the result as a very interesting connection nonetheless!

## Tangent Sets

@thm-RAL-IFs holds simultaneously for *all* differentiable paths in the model through $\p$ (and all their induced scores). To unlock the important insights from the theorem we therefore need to be able to refer to that set of scores.

:::: callout-note
# Tangent Set

::: {#def-tangent-set}
The *tangent set* $\tset_\p$ at a point $\p \in \model$ is the set of all scores of all differentiable paths through that point. When the point of interest $\p$ is clear from context we leave the subscript off and just write $\tset$ for the tangent set.

$\tset_{\p} \subseteq \{f \in \eltwop: \p f = 0\} \equiv \eltwopz$ since any score $s$ of a differentiable path through $\p$ is in $\eltwop$ and has mean zero by @def-score.
:::
::::

Very often the tangent set is a closed vector space (i.e. it is closed under sums, scaling, and limits; see @def-vector-space). When this is the case, some authors refer to the tangent set as the tangent *space*. If the tangent set is not already a closed vector space, the term "tangent space" usually refers to the linear closure of the tangent set (all linear combinations of scores and their $\eltwo$-limits).

::: {#fig-tangent-set}

A visual representation of the tangent set $\tset$ along with the model $\sqrt{\model}$, two differentiable paths, and two scores (times $\sqrt p$). The set $\tset \sqrt{p}$ denotes the set of all scores times the root density: $\{s \sqrt{p}: s \in \tset\}$.
:::

Looking at @fig-tangent-set, it's clear why we call this the the "tangent" set: the plane $\tset_\p \sqrt p$ is tangent to the surface of the root-model $\sqrt{\model}$ at the density $\sqrt p$. That is also why we use the evocative dot notation for the tangent set: $\tset_\p \sqrt p$ contains all of the derivatives $\overset{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}{\sqrt{p_\epsilon}}$. Although the picture in fact shows the root-model and tangent set times the root density, we often say informally that the tangent set $\tset_{\p}$ itself is "tangent" to the model $\model$ at the distribution $\p$.

Since it's useful to think of scores as directions we can move away from $\p$ in the model, the tangent set is simply the set of all such directions. If a model is "large" in a neighborhood of $\p$ in the sense that there are many directions you can go in and stay in the model, then the tangent set will be large. If a model is "small" around $\p$ then the tangent set will be small.

:::: {#exm-tangent-set-normal}
Consider the model $\model = \{\norm(\mu,\sigma^2): \mu \in \reals, \sigma^2 > 0\}$ with densities $p_{\mu,\sigma^2}(z)$ and the point $\p = \norm(0,1)$ with density $p(z) = (2\pi)^{-1/2} e^{-{z^2}/{2}}$ of the standard normal. Since this is a two-dimensional parametric model, the tangent set at $p$ is all linear combinations of

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_\mu(z) &= \left. \frac{\partial p_{\mu,\sigma^2}(z)}{\partial \mu} \right|_{\mu=0, \sigma^2=1} = z \\
s_{\sigma^2}(z)  &= \left. \frac{\partial p_{\mu,\sigma^2}(z)}{\partial \sigma^2} \right|_{\mu=0, \sigma^2 =1} = \frac{z^2 -1}{2} \\
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus in this case $\tset$ is a two-dimensional set of functions.

::: {#fig-parametric-tangent-sets}

``` tikz
  \shade[top color=gray!30, bottom color=white] (bottomleft) rectangle ($(bottomright)-(0,0.5)$);
  \shade[left color=gray!30, right color=white] (bottomright) rectangle ($(topright)+(0.5,0)$);
  \shade[shading=fast, shading angle=-45]  ($(topright)-(0.01,0.01)$) rectangle ($(topright)+(0.5,0.5)$);
  \shade[shading=fast, shading angle=-135] ($(bottomright)+(-0.01,0.01)$) rectangle ($(bottomright)+(0.5,-0.5)$);
  \node[gray, below right, font=\Large] at ($(bottomright)+(-0.2,0.2)$) {$\mathcal P$};

  % small coordinate axis at left-middle of rectangle
  \begin{scope}[shift={(0,0)}]
    \draw[->, thick] (0,0) -- (0,0.6) node[right,font=\small] {$\mu$};
    \draw[->, thick] (0,0) -- (0.6,0) node[below,font=\small] {$\sigma^2$};
    \fill (0,0) circle (1pt);
  \end{scope}

  \begin{scope}[shift={(1.3,0)}]
     \draw[->, gray, very thick] (0,0) -- ++(-0,1.7) node[below right] {$\mathcal P_{\mu+}$};
      % three small arrows emanating from that point
      \draw[->, blue] (0,0) -- ++(0.3,0.05);
      \draw[->, blue] (0,0) -- ++(-0.2,0.3);
      \draw[->, blue] (0,0) -- ++(-0.1,-0.25);
      \draw[->, orange, thick] (0,0) -- ++(0,+0.4);

    \filldraw[black] (0,0) circle (2pt) node[above right,font=\small] {$\mathcal N(0,1)$};

```

A cartoon representation of the models $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal P_{\mu +}$ discussed in this example. The arrows emanating from $\norm(0,1)$ indicate scores of paths in $\mathcal P$, but only the orange arrow is a score of a path in $\mathcal P_{\mu +}$.
:::

If we instead restricted the model to be $\model_\mu = \{\norm(\mu,1): \mu \in \reals\}$ by fixing $\sigma^2 =1$ (presume we knew this a-priori), then the tangent set would be all linear combinations of $s_\mu$ alone, i,e, $\{cs_\mu: c \in \reals\}$, a one-dimensional subset of the tangent set for the larger model.

Lastly, if we considered the even smaller model $\model_{\mu+} = \{\norm(\mu,1): \mu \ge 0\}$, then the point $\p = \norm(0,1)$ would be on the "edge" of this model. Consequently there is no differentiable path that goes in the "negative $\mu$" direction from $\p$ and therefore the tangent set would be restricted to $\{cs_\mu: c \ge 0\}$, again a subset of the tangent space in the larger parent model. On the other hand, if we considered the point $\p = \norm(1,1)$ in this same model, the tangent space set would be $\{cs_\mu: c \in \reals\}$, the same as in the larger model where $\mu$ is allowed to be negative. This is because $\norm(1,1)$ is in the "interior" of the restricted model, so the mean can be decreased without any problem.
::::

This example demonstrates why the tangent set is specific to a particular point in a particular model. The notation $\tset_{\p}$ makes the model dependence very explicit and that is why I prefer it to something more cumbersome like $\mathcal S_{\model, \p}$. The tangent set depends crucially on where the point is within the model because that affects what directions it is legal to move in while remaining in the model (recall that paths are subsets of the model). The shape and size of the tangent set is determined entirely by the *local* character of the model at $\p$. We saw in the example above that the tangent set at $\norm(0,1)$ became smaller if we restricted the mean in the normal model to be non-negative, but at $\norm(1,1)$ the tangent set was unaffected by that restriction. There are many more examples of specific tangent sets in Chapters 3 and 4 of @bkrw but for now we can proceed with the intuition we have without getting bogged down in details.

In @def-tangent-set we noted that $\tset_{\p} \subseteq \eltwopz$ (recall we defined this as the set of $\eltwop$ functions with $\p$-mean zero). Some models are so "large", however, that the inclusion is actually an equality. If the model is big enough (locally), you can move in any direction.

::: {#exm-tangent-set-nonparam}
Let $\mathcal p$ be the set of all distributions of continuous random variables (i.e. distributions with standard densities) and pick some point $\p \in \model$. For any bounded function $s \in \eltwopz$ we can construct the convex path $p_\eps = (1+ \eps s) p_0$ (bounding $s$ is required so that $p_\eps$ remains a density and the mean-square and pointwise scores coincide). As we saw in @exm-convex-path-score, $s$ is the score for such a path at $\p$ and thus the tangent set at that point includes at least all bounded functions $s \in \eltwopz$.

This is good enough for intuition, but to remove the boundedness condition on the scores and formally extend to all $\eltwopz$ we can instead use the paths $p_\eps = \frac{e^{\lambda(\eps s)}}{\int e^{\lambda(\eps s(z))} p_0(z) \dd z} p_0$ with $\lambda(t) = 2(1+e^{-2t})^{-1}$. These paths also have scores $s$ and generate valid densities for any $s \in \eltwopz$. For details see Example 1 in Chapter 3 of @bkrw.
:::

We give this kind of model its own name.

:::: callout-note
# Locally Nonparametric Model

::: {#def-nonparam-model}
A model $\model$ is *locally nonparametric* at $\p \in \model$ if $\tset_{\p} = \eltwopz$.
:::
::::

This is the kind of model we will work with most often for the remainder of this book. Locally nonparametric models are popular in practice because they enforce essentially no assumptions on the data-generating distribution. In fields like medicine, economics, or business, we often cannot say much about the world with great confidence (the distribution of variables, the functional form of their relationships, etc.). We will see shortly that the larger the model is, usually the more uncertainty we get in the final estimate. This makes sense: the more assumptions you're willing to make, the more confident you can be of an estimate. But if you use a model that is too small (i.e. assume things that are not actually true) then the estimate may be biased and confidence intervals will typically underestimate the true sampling uncertainty. Working with a locally nonparametric model is therefore a maximally robust approach, or at worst conservative.

### Factoring

There are, of course, many practical situations where we *do* know something. For example, in our familiar covariate-treatment-outcome $(X,A,Y)$ setup, if the treatment is allocated randomly by coin flip, then we know for a fact that $\p(A=1|X) = 1/2$. This is an important restriction on the model. Due to the ability to experimentally control treatment assignments, there are many cases in causal inference where one or more factors of a probability distribution are known exactly, but nothing is certain about the others. Thankfully, it's not hard to figure out the tangent set in such models.

To simplify things, we'll work in a generic model defined over two variables $(Y,Z)$ (you can think of $Z=(A,X)$ if you please). We'll also presume again that all our distributions have densities and that the pointwise definition of the scores coincides with the mean-square derivative definition to facilitate the explanation. All of the results below also hold in the mean-square sense of scores in models without densities but everything is more cumbersome to prove without adding any intuition. I've put sketches of those proofs into boxed-off sections that you can safely ignore.

Since every distribution $\p(Y,Z)$ can be factored into $\p(Y,Z) = \p(Y|Z) \p(Z)$, every differentiable path of distributions $\p^{(\eps)}(Y,Z)$ induces a path of marginal distributions $\p^{(\eps)}(Z)$ and a path of conditional distributions $\p^{(\eps)}(Y|Z)$. Let's pick some arbitrary path with score $s$. We can take derivatives of the log-likelihoods along the induced conditional and marginal paths to obtain scores (in terms of the pointwise definition):

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_Z(z) &= \partial_0 \log p_\eps(z) \\
s_{Y|Z}(y,z) &= \partial_0 \log p_\eps(y|z)
\end{aligned}
$$

where I'm abbreviating the operator $\left. \frac{\dd}{\dd \eps} \right|_{\eps=0} (\cdot)$ with $\partial_0 (\cdot)$. When the meaning is clear from context I'll abuse notation a bit and write $s(z)$ for $s_Z(z)$ and similarly $s(y|z)$ for $s_{Y|Z}(y,z)$, the same way as is usually done for marginal and conditional density functions. If we iterate this over all differentiable paths and collect the resulting scores we generate what I'll call the marginal and conditional tangent sets $\tset_\p(Z)$ and $\tset_\p(Y|Z)$.

Let's see how these marginal and conditional scores are related to the joint score for a given path. First off, because

$$
\log p_\eps(z,y) = \log (p_\eps(y|z) p_\eps(z)) = \log p_\eps(y|z) + \log p_\eps(z),
$$

when we apply $\partial_0$ to both sides we get

$$
s(y,z) = s(y|z) + s(z)
$$

so the joint score is simply the sum of the marginal and conditional scores. But we can further characterize these scores in terms of the joint score. By the chain rule, $\partial \log p_\eps = \frac{\partial p_\eps}{p_\eps}$, so evaluating at $\eps = 0$ and shifting terms around gives

$$
\partial_0 p_\eps = p_0 \partial_0 p_\eps = p_0 s.
$$ {#eq-score-deriv}

This is true for the joint, conditional, and marginal densities/scores. If we start with this equation in terms of the joint density/score and integrate with respect to $y$ on both sides we have

$$
\int \partial_0 p_\eps(y,z) \dd y = \int p_0(y,z) s(y,z) \dd y.
$$

On the left-hand-side, if we are allowed to exchange integration w.r.t $z$ and differentiation w.r.t. $\epsilon$ (formally this is possible under mild restrictions on the model), then we get $\partial_0 \int p_\eps(y,z) \dd y = \partial_0 p_\eps(z) = p_0(z) s(z)$ by applying @eq-score-deriv to the marginal $p_\eps(z)$. Dividing both sides of the above by $p_0(z)$ gives

$$
s(z) = \int \frac{p_0(y,z)}{p_0(z)} s(y,z) \dd y = \int p(y|z) s(y,z) \dd y = \E[s(Y,Z)|Z=z]
$$

and therefore $s(y|z) = s(y,z) - \E[s(Y,Z)|Z=z]$ since the conditional and marginal scores sum to the joint.

We now have explicit formulations of the marginal and conditional scores in terms of the joint score. Besides their relation to the joint score, these scores also have some interesting properties. You may recall from @def-score that $\p s = 0$, i.e. $\E[s(Y,Z)] = 0$. The conditional and joint score obey similar conditions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E[s(Z)] &= 0 \\
\E[s(Y|Z)| Z] &= 0. \\
\end{aligned}
$$

The first identity comes from the explicit definition of $s(z)$ because $\E_Z[s(Z)] = \E_Z[\E_Y[s(Y,Z)|Z]] = \E[s(Y,Z)] = 0$ by total expectation and since the joint score is mean zero. The second comes from

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E_Y[s(Y|Z)| Z] 
&= \E_Y[s(Y,Z) - \E_Y[s(Y,Z)|Z] | Z] \\
&=\E_Y[s(Y,Z)|Z]- \E_Y[s(Y,Z)|Z]
\end{aligned}
$$

We can also show that the marginal and conditional score functions are orthogonal to each other in $\eltwop$. Recall that two functions are orthogonal if their inner product is zero and that the $\eltwop$ inner product of two functions is the expectation of their product (see @sec-app-L2). The expected value of the product of the conditional and marginal scores is

$$
\E[s(Z)s(Y|Z)] 
= \E[\E[s(Y,Z)|Z] (s(Y,Z) - \E[s(Y,Z)|Z] )].
$$

Abbreviating $S = s(Y,Z)$, by total expectation, $\E[\E_S[S|Z] S] = \E_Z[\E_S[\E_S[S|Z] S | Z]] = \E_Z[\E_S[S|Z] \E_S[ S | Z]]$ so the above is zero.

This is actually a general fact about conditional expectation that is used in many places throughout probability theory: a random variable minus its conditional expectation is orthogonal to that conditional expectation. In fact, the conditional expectation $\E[f(Y,Z)|Z]$ of a random variable $f(Y,Z)$ is precisely its orthogonal projection onto the subspace spanned by all $\eltwop$ functions of $Z$ alone: the best possible $\eltwop$ approximation of $f(y,z)$ that can be attained with functions of $z$. This is illustrated in @fig-conditional-scores.

::: {#fig-conditional-scores}
``` tikz
\tdplotsetmaincoords{60}{60}
\resizebox{12cm}{!}{
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=3,tdplot_main_coords]

  % Draw small 3D axes
  \draw[->] (0,0,0) -- (1,0,0) node[anchor=north east]{};
  \draw[->] (0,0,0) -- (0,1,0) node[anchor=north west]{};
  \draw[->] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,1) node[anchor=south]{};

  % Shaded plane: functions of Z alone (the xy-plane)
  \filldraw[fill=blue!10,draw=blue!50,opacity=0.4]
    (-0.5,-0.5,0) -- (1,-0.5,0) -- (1,1,0) -- (-0.5,1,0) -- cycle;
  \node at (0.5,-0.6,0) [blue!50, anchor=south]{$\{\text{functions of z alone}\}$};

  % Define vector s_{Y,Z}
  \coordinate (v) at (0.7,0.5,0.8);
  \draw[->,thick] (0,0,0) -- (v) node[midway,above]{$s_{Y,Z}$};

  % Orthogonal projection onto plane (drop z-coordinate)
  \coordinate (p) at (0.7,0.5,0);
  \draw[->, thick, densely dashed, blue] (0,0,0) -- (p) node[blue, midway,below]{$s_Z$};
  % Dashed line from vector tip down to projection
  \draw[dotted] (v) -- (p);

  % Residual vector from projection to original vector
  \draw[->,thick, orange, dash pattern=on 3pt off 1pt] (p) -- (v) node[midway,right]{$s_{Y\mid Z}$};

    % Origin label
  \node at (0,0,0.5) [anchor=north east]{$\mathcal L_2^0(\mathbb{P}(Y,Z))$};
\end{tikzpicture}
}
```

The marginal score is an orthogonal projection of the joint score and the conditional score is the residual.
:::

Let's summarize all these results.

:::: callout-note
# Conditional and Marginal Scores

::: {#thm-conditional-scores}
Let $\model = \model(Y,Z)$ be a model over joint distributions $\p(Y,Z)$ of variables $(Y,Z)$ and let $\model_{\eps}(Y,Z)$ be a differentiable path with score $s(y,z)$. This path induces marginal and conditional paths $\model_{\eps}(Z)$ and $\model_{\eps}(Y|Z)$ with scores

$$
\begin{aligned}
s(z) &= \E[s(Y,Z)|Z] \\
s(y|z) &= s(y,z) - \E[s(Y,Z)|Z] \\
\end{aligned}
$$

which sum to $s(y,z)$. The marginal score $s_Z$ is the orthogonal projection of the joint score $s_{Y,Z}$ onto the span of all $\eltwop$ functions of $z$ alone, while the conditional score $z_{Y|Z}$ is the residual of this projection. Therefore $s_{Y|Z} \perp s_Z$ in $\eltwop$. Moreover

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E[s(Z)] &= 0 \\
\E[s(Y|Z)| Z] &= 0, \\
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
# Proof Sketch for Mean-Square Scores

Let $\model_\eps$ be a (mean-square) differentiable path over distributions $\p(Y,Z)$ and let $\eps_n \to 0$ and $\p_n = \p_{\eps_n}$ be a sequence along the path with $\p = \p_{\eps=0}$. Let $\q(Y,Z)$ be a dominating measure constructed for the sequence $\p_n$ and let $p_n(y,z) = \frac{\dd \p_n(Y,Z)}{\dd \q(Y,Z)}$ be densities. Let $Q(Z)$ and $\p(Z)$ be the marginal distributions of $\q(Y,Z)$ and $\p(Y,Z)$, respectively, so that $p_n(z) = \frac{\dd \p_n(Z)}{\dd \q(Z)}$ are marginal densities.

Since the path of joint distributions is differentiable, there is a function $g(y,z)$ such that

$$
\left\|
\frac{\sqrt{p_n(y,z)} - \sqrt{p_0(y,z)}}{\eps_n} - g(y,z)
\right\|_{\eltwop[\q(Y,Z)]} \to 0
$$

Our goal is to show that the path of marginal distributions is also differentiable, i.e. that there is a function $g(z)$ for which

$$
\left\|
\frac{\sqrt{p_n(z)} - \sqrt{p(z)}}{\eps_n} - g(z)
\right\|_{\eltwop[\q(Z)]} \to 0
$$

First decompose

$$
\sqrt{p_n(z)} - \sqrt{p(z)} = \frac{p_n(z) - p(z)}{\sqrt{p_n(z)} + \sqrt{p(z)}}
$$

and notice that, by definition,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_n(z) - \p(z)
&=
\int p_n(y,z) - p(y,z) \dd \q(Y|Z) \\
&= 
\int \left(\sqrt{p_n(y,z)} - \sqrt{p(y,z)}\right) \left(\sqrt{p_n(y,z)} + \sqrt{p(y,z)}\right) \dd \q(Y|Z)
.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equivalent of the more familiar formula $p(z) = \int p (y,z) \dd y$ except that in this case we do not assume that $\q$ is a product measure. In the familiar case we see $\dd y = \dd \mu(Y)$ because $\dd \mu(Y) = \dd \mu(Y|Z)$, i.e. Lebesgue measure is a product measure.

Combining these observations,

$$
\frac{\sqrt{p_n(z)} - \sqrt{p(z)}}{\eps_n}
= 
\int \underbrace{\frac{\sqrt{p_n(y,z)} - \sqrt{p(y,z)}}{\eps_n}}_{g_n(y,z)}  \underbrace{\frac{\sqrt{p_n(y,z)} + \sqrt{p(y,z)}}{\sqrt{p_n(z)} + \sqrt{p(z)}}}_{h_n(y,z)}  \dd \q(Y|Z).
$$

$g_n \overset{\eltwop[Q(Y,Z)]}\to g$ by assumption and since $\sqrt{p_n(y,z)} \overset{\eltwop[Q(Y,Z)]} \to \sqrt{p(y,z)}$, the second factor $h_n$ can be shown to converge in $\eltwop[Q(Y,Z)]$ to $h(y,z) = \sqrt{p(y,z)/p(z)} = \sqrt{p(y|z)}$ with careful handling of the denominator.

Therefore one might conjecture that the $\eltwop[Q(Z)]$ limit of the above is $\int g(y,z) h(y,z) \dd \q(Y|Z)$ and indeed this is the case because

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int \left(
\int g_n h_n - gh \dd \q(Y|Z)
\right)^2 
\dd \q(Z) 
&\le 
\int 
\int (g_n h_n - gh)^2 \dd \q(Y|Z)
\dd \q(Z) \\
&=
\int (g_n h_n - gh)^2 \dd \q(Y,Z)
\to 0
\end{aligned}
$$

by Jensen's inequality ($0 \le \V[U] = \E[U^2] - \E[U]^2 \implies \E[U]^2 < \E[U^2]$) and the aforementioned convergences.

This shows that $g(z) = \int g(y,z) \sqrt{p(y|z)} \dd Q(Y|Z)$. Defining $s(z) = 2 g(z) / \sqrt{p(z)}$ and $s(y,z) = 2 g(y,z) / \sqrt{p(y,z)}$ gives

$$
s(z) = \int s(y,z) p(y|z) \dd Q(Y|Z) = \int s(y,z) \dd P(Y|Z) = \E[s(Y,Z)|Z=z].
$$

Similar arguments may be used to derive the conditional score $s(y|z)$ and then the other facts follow algebraically.
:::

Given this characterization, it's easy to derive the tangent set of a model that has a restricted factor. In a model with a restricted factor, paths can only change the other factors and the scores are the "directions" that change only the non-restricted factors. For example if $p(z)$ is fixed in the model but $p(y|z)$ is free, then the scores are $s(y,z) = s(y|z) + 0$, i.e. the $z$-component $s(z)=0$ is fixed at $0$ so as to not change the fixed marginal density $p(z)$.

:::: callout-note
# Tangent Sets in Factored Models

::: {#thm-factored-tset}
Let $\model$ be locally nonparametric around some distribution $\p(Y,Z) = \p(Y|Z)\p(Z)$.

Let $\model^{(Z)} = \{\p(Y|Z)\tilde\p(Z): \tilde\p \in \model\}$, be a restriction of the original model where all the conditional distributions $\p(Y|Z)$ are replaced with the fixed conditional distribution $\p(Y|Z)$, but the marginal distributions of $Z$ are allowed to vary. Then the tangent set at $\p$ in the restricted model is the set of all $Z$-marginal scores in the original model, i.e.

$$
\tset^{(Z)}_\p = \tset_\p (Z),
$$

which is all $\eltwopz$ functions of $z$ alone.

Similarly, if $\model^{(Y|Z)} = \{\tilde\p(Y|Z)\p(Z): \tilde\p \in \model\}$, a mutation of the original model where all the *marginal* distributions are fixed, but the *conditional* distributions can still vary, then

$$
\tset^{(Y|Z)}_\p = \tset_\p (Y|Z),
$$

which is all $\eltwopz$ functions of $(y,z)$ with $z$-conditional mean zero.
:::
::::

## Pathwise Differentiability

Now that we understand a bit more about the set of all scores we can return to the central identity above (definition @thm-RAL-IFs). By comparing the asymptotic behavior while moving quickly along differentiable paths implied by regularity to the behavior implied by asymptotic linearity, we deduced that any RAL estimator (with influence function $\phi$) satisfies

$$
\dot\Psi_\p s = \p s\phi
$$

for any differentiable path through $\p$ with score $s$. In other words, that equality is satisfied for all scores $s \in \tset_\p$, the tangent set of the model $\model$ at the distribution $\p$.

Let's dig into the left-hand term:

$$
\dot\Psi_{\p} (s) \overset{\mathrm{def}} 
= \lim_{\eps \to 0} \frac{\Psi(\p^{(\eps)}) - \Psi(\p^{(0)})}{\eps}
= \left. \frac{\dd}{\dd \eps} \right|_{\eps=0} \Psi(\p^{(\eps)}) 
.
$$

For any fixed path this is a standard, vanilla derivative of a one-dimensional function of $\epsilon$. It measures the (instantaneous) rate of change of the estimand as we shift the underlying distribution along the path away from $\eps=0$. This is illustrated in @fig-pathwise-derivative.

::: {#fig-pathwise-derivative}

``` tikz
  \coordinate (shape11) at ($(shape11Base) + (0,\BlobYShift)$);
  \coordinate (shape12) at ($(shape12Base) + (0,\BlobYShift)$);

  \coordinate (xAxisEnd)   at ( 1.25,3.50);

  \coordinate (yAxisEnd)   at ( 0.00,5.05);

  };

  %--- Blob region \mathcal{P} (outline) ---

    plot[smooth cycle, tension=0.7] coordinates {

    };

  %--- Internal path \mathcal{P}_\epsilon ---
  \draw[blue, dashed, line width=1.2pt]
    plot[smooth] coordinates {
      (blobCtrl1) (blobZero) (blobCtrl2)
    };
  % Label for \mathcal{P}_\epsilon shifted with the blob
  \node[blue, left] at (blobCtrl1) {$\mathcal{P}_\epsilon$};

  % Tangent arrow s on the internal path at \epsilon=0
  \draw[blue, ->, line width=1.2pt] (blobZero) -- ++(0.40,0.05) node[right] {\small $s$};

  % Mark \epsilon=0 on the internal path
  \fill[black] (blobZero) circle (0.04);
  \node[below] at (blobZero) {\small $\mathbb P$};

  %--- Dotted vertical connectors from the x-axis down to the shifted blob points ---
  \draw[gray!60, dotted] (xNegTop)  -- (blobCtrl1);
  \draw[gray!60, dotted] (xZeroTop) -- (blobZero);
  \draw[gray!60, dotted] (xPosTop)  -- (blobCtrl2);

```

The pathwise derivative evaluated at a particular score $s$ gives the rate of change of the estimand if we move the underlying distribution in the direction of (and at the speed of) the score.
:::

However, that slope is generally different depending on the path one chooses. There may be paths along with the estimand is increasing rapidly, paths along which it is decreasing, and paths along which it is constant. Moreover if you "accelerate" the speed at which a path goes by multiplying the score by some value $c >1$, the derivative will also be magnified. That is why we write $\dot\Psi_{\p}(s)$ as a function of $s$, the "direction" (and "speed") of the path. Since the slope is taken at $\epsilon=0$, the only thing that matters is the immediate direction of the path at $\p$, i.e. the score $s$. The instantaneous rate of change of the estimand along two different paths with the same score will be the same. Because it is a derivative along a path, we aptly call the function $s \mapsto \dot\Psi_\p(s)$ mapping from $\tset_\p$ to $\reals$ the *pathwise derivative* of the estimand $\Psi$ at the distribution $\p$ in the model $\model$*.*

The identity $\dot\Psi_\p (s) = \p s\phi$ says that the slope $\dot\Psi_{\p}(s)$ may be found by taking the inner product of $s$ with *any* influence function $\phi$ of a RAL estimator. In fact, it doesn't matter *which* RAL estimator, if there are multiple: the result must be the same. We'll return to this point in the next section but we are actually getting ahead of ourselves because we are assuming there *is* a RAL estimator. The argument for @thm-RAL-IFs only established a condition that must be met by any RAL estimator, not that such an estimator exists. In fact, the result implies something about when RAL estimators *can* exist.

Notice that on the right-hand side, $\p s \phi$ is an inner product. Seen as a function $s \mapsto \p s\phi$ acting on the tangent set $\tset_\p$, the inner product is a bounded (i.e. continuous) linear functional (see @def-bounded-functional and @exm-cont-inner-prod). Informally, a small change in the input score must always translate to a small change in the inner product with the fixed function $\phi$. Since this inner product is equal to the pathwise derivative, that implies that the pathwise derivative must *also* be linear and continuous in the same sense: if we look at two paths that go in similar directions, the rate of change of the estimand must be similar on those paths.

The interesting thing is that the pathwise derivative has nothing to do with the estimator: it is defined purely by the model $\model$, the distribution $\p$ of interest within it, and the estimand $\Psi$. The pathwise derivative either exists and is linear and continuous across scores or it isn't. If it isn't a continuous linear functional, then it's not possible for it to be equal to any inner product. But since that equality must hold for any RAL estimator, if the pathwise derivative is not a continuous linear functional, then there cannot be any RAL estimator for that estimand in that model in the first place.

:::: callout-note
# Pathwise Differentiability

::: {#def-pathwise-differentiability}
An estimand $\Psi$ is *pathwise differentiable* at $\p \in \model$ if the pathwise derivative $\dot\Psi_\p$ exists and is linear and continuous across the tangent set $\mathcal P_\p$.

If an estimand is not pathwise differentiable, there is no asymptotically linear estimator that is regular in that model.
:::
::::

::: callout-warning
Review @def-continuity for the definition of continuity and @sec-app-riesz for details and definitions relating to Hilbert spaces and Riesz representation. Understanding the details is not nearly as important as understanding the big-picture implications here so it's ok if you skip the mathematical details for now and come back to them on a second pass later.
:::

It's sometimes helpful to think of the pathwise derivative as the best continuous, linear approximation to $\Psi(\p)$ at the point $\p$, the same way that a tangent plane locally approximates the surface of a real-valued function of two or more variables. In this analogy, the tangent plane should itself be thought of as a function (a continuous and linear one) defined on the same variables.

::: callout-note
The analogy is somehwat imprecise because for a standard derivative of a function $f(z)$ with vector inputs, the "tangent plane" $\dot f(h) \approx f(z+h) - f(z)$ is defined on the same input vector space as the function itself, i.e. $h$ and $z$ are elements of the same vector space. For the pathwise derivative, the equivalent approximation is $\dot\Psi(s) \approx \Psi(\p^{(\eps)}) - \Psi(\p)$, but $\p$ and $s$ are two different kinds of objects. The trouble is that distributions in a model don't naturally form a vector space: we can embedd them into $\eltwo$ as root-densities by assuming they are dominated by some other measure but at a loss of generality.

If that is done, however, then the pathwise derivative corresponds exactly with something called a Hadamard derivative. This kind of derivative is slightly weaker than the standard (total) derivative (called a Fréchet derivative). Roughly speaking, the usual total derivative tangent plane must approximate the error $\dot f(h) \approx f(z+h)$ for any sequence $h$ approaching in any directions to $0$, whereas the Hadamard derivative only needs to give the right approximation along sequences $h$ that eventually settle into a single directional approach to zero. Roughly speaking, this corresponds to the pathwise derivative because the latter is only concerned with sequences along differentiable paths, i.e. paths where the difference of subsequent steps is eventually well-approximated by the "direction" function $s$ (the score).

It is not necessary, however, to make assumptions in order to embed the model into $\eltwo$. The pathwise derivative as given in @thm-RAL-IFs and @def-pathwise-differentiability works just fine in generic models. While most similar to the Hadamard derivative, it does not precisely correspond to any form of derivative that is defined on vector spaces.
:::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-pathwise-deriv-figure}
On a piece of paper sketch out a replica of @fig-tangent-set.

a.  Draw some curvy, smooth level sets of your choosing over the surface of $\sqrt{\model}$ representing the value of $\Psi(\p)$ at each point. One of your level set lines should pass through the point $\sqrt p$.
b.  Draw some straight, evenly spaced level-set lines across $\sqrt p \tset$ representing the value of $\dot\Psi(s)$ at each point (you can peek at @fig-gradient to see what I mean). One of the level-set lines should pass through $\sqrt p$ and at that point should be tangent to the level set of $\Psi$ passing through $\sqrt p$ on $\sqrt{\model}$.

Your drawing represents the sense in which $\dot\Psi$ is a local, linear approximation to $\Psi: \model \to \reals$. If you imagine zooming into the point $\sqrt p \in \sqrt{\model}$ the surface of the sphere begins to look essentially flat (like the tangent set) and the curves of the contours on the model also flatten out into a regular linear pattern. The flattening of the model is due to the differentiability of the paths whereas the flattening of the level sets are due to pathwise differentiability of the estimand.
:::
::::

A pathwise-differentiable estimand "varies smoothly" over the model the same way that a ordinary function with a continuous derivative has no kinks. At any point of a kink or discontinuity in the estimand, no estimator can be regular.

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-discontinuous-estimand}
Let $Z$ be normally distributed with known variance $1$ but unknown mean $\mu$, i.e. $\model = \{\norm(\mu,1):\mu \in \reals\}$. Presume we are interested in estimating the quantity $\Psi(\p) = 1(\E_\p[Z] > 0)$, i.e. whether the mean is positive or not (we are estimating, not testing).

a.  Draw a plot of the function $\mu \mapsto \Psi(\norm(\mu,1))$
b.  At $\p = \norm(0,1)$, do you think $\Psi$ is pathwise differentiable? If not, is it because the derivative doesn't exist or is it because the derivative isn't continuous?
c.  Repeat the above for the new estimand $\Psi(\p) = |\E_\p[Z]|$.
d.  Let $\hat\mu =\frac{1}{n} \sum Z_i$. What are the sampling distributions of $1(\hat\mu > 0)$ and $\left| \hat\mu \right|$ when $Z \sim \norm(0,1)$?

This exercise shows that some simple estimands are not pathwise differentiable, although the examples are somewhat contrived because in both cases it would be more natural to estimate $\mu$ and then perform a hypothesis test. On the other hand, it also shows that lacking pathwise differentiability need not be the end of the world: both of the estimands have natural, easily-understood estimators that would be hard to beat in practice even in nonparametric models.
:::
::::

The examples in @exr-discontinuous-estimand are contrived. More often the types of "kinks" or discontinuities that cause problems are difficult to visualize in lower-dimensions. It's not as if the value of most practically interesting non-differentiable estimands changes suddenly as we move along a single differentiable path. The fact that the path is differentiable means that the densities change smoothly as we walk in that fixed direction and that usually implies smooth behavior of the estimand along a given path. 

The kinks are sometimes only visible "rotationally". I like to imagine standing at a point $\p$ on the "surface" $\Psi(\p)$ and looking in some direction: I imagine seeing how steep the ascent or descent is in whatever direction I look. The problem with most practically interesting estimands that are not differentiable isn't that there is a discontinuity or kink in any given direction, it's that no matter what direction you look at, there is always another direction where the slope is steeper. But an estimand is pathwise differentiable at a point in a model only if there is a "direction of maximum slope" away from that point. In infinite dimensions, kinks occur in this "rotational" sense more often than they occur in the more familiar one-dimension sense.

::: {#exm-unbounded-estimand}
Let $\mathcal P$ be all distributions of a continuous variable $Z$. Let's say that our goal is to estimate the value of the density function of $z$ at the point $z=0$. There generally isn't a good motivation for wanting to know this, it's just a simple example that illustrates ideas that apply identically to more complicated estimands.

We'll show that there is no RAL estimator of the density at a point by establishing that the pathwise derivative is not bounded over the tangent set $\tset_\p$ (at any $\p$). The intuition is that we can find a path that comes very, very close to modifying the density *only* at the point $z=0$. In other words, we can modify the estimand by arbitrary amounts essentially without changing the overall density.

Fix a distribution $\p$. Since the model is nonparametric, the tangent set $\tset_\p$ is all of $\eltwopz$. Since that's the case, any zero-mean $\eltwop$ function can be a score.

Define the sequence of probabilities $t_n = \p\{-1/n \le Z \le 1/n\}$. Since these are probabilities of smaller and smaller sets over a continuous random variable they must shrink to zero.

We'll consider a sequence of scores

$$
s_n(z) = \frac{1\left(-\frac{1}{n} \le z \le \frac{1}{n}\right) - t_n}{\sqrt{t_n(1-t_n)}}
$$

The random variable $1(-1/n \le Z \le 1/n)$ is $1$ with probability $t_n$ and $0$ with probability $1-t_n$, i.e. it is $\bern(t_n)$. Therefore it has mean $t_n$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{t_n(1-t_n)}$. Consequently, the mean of $s_n(Z)$ is zero and its standard deviation ($\eltwop$ norm) is $1$. Thus $s_n$ are all $\eltwop$ functions with mean zero as desired, i.e. these are scores in the tangent set $\tset_\p$. Moreover these are unit-norm scores.

To find the pathwise derivatives $\dot\Psi(s_n)$, let's consider a sequence of paths $\model_\eps^{(n)}$ that have the desired scores. For this we can use the convex paths $p_\eps^{(n)} = (1+\eps s_n)p$ that we previously used in @exm-path-convex and @exm-convex-path-score. Now we can evaluate the pathwise derivative directly:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot\Psi(s_n) 
&= \left. \frac{\dd}{\dd \eps} \right|_{\eps=0} \Psi(\p^{(\eps)}) \\
&= \left. \frac{\dd}{\dd \eps} \right|_{\eps=0} (1+\eps s_n(0))p(0) \\
&= s_n(0) p(0) \\
&= \frac{1 - t_n}{\sqrt{t_n(1-t_n)}} p(0) \\
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t_n$ converges to zero, the denominator blows up. Since we only considered unit scores, we proved that there is no pure direction of maximum increase: no matter what direction we look, there is always another direction for which the pathwise derivative is bigger. Therefore the pathwise derivative is unbounded (not continuous). As a consequence, there can be no RAL estimator for the density at a point when the model is all continuous densities.

With more setup and more care taken to define tangent sets, etc., very similar arguments apply if we are estimating the value of a prediction function at a point (i.e. $\E[Y|X=x]$) or a conditional average treatment effect ($\E[Y|X=x,A=1] - \E[Y|X=x,A=0]$) in nonparametric models. These are important examples of practically relevant estimands for which there are no RAL estimators! The theory we develop in the rest of this book does not apply to these estimands which is why approaches to estimate them can be more ad-hoc, context dependent, and difficult to build formal inference around.
:::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-density-at-point-normal-location}
Whether an estimand is pathwise differentiable or not depends on the model. Imagine that we know $Z$ is normally distributed with known variance $1$ but unknown mean $\mu$, i.e. $\model = \{\norm(\mu,1):\mu \in \reals\}$ and we are interested in estimating the value of the density $p(z)$ at the point $z=0$. This is again a contrived example but the point is to illustrate ideas in the simplest setting possible. Recall that the density of a $\norm(\mu,1)$ random variable is $p(z) = (2\pi)^{-1/2} e^{-(z-\mu)^2/2}$.

a.  What is the tangent set $\tset_\p$ at any point $\p$ in this model? What is the dimension of this tangent set?
b.  For any score $s \in \tset_\p$, construct the convex path $p_\eps = (1+\eps s)p$ and use it to compute the pathwise derivative $\dot\Psi(s)$.
c.  What is $\dot\Psi(s)/ \|s\|$? According to @def-bounded-functional and @def-pathwise-differentiability what does this imply about the pathwise differentiability of the estimand in this model?
d.  Can you guess what a RAL estimator of $p(0)$ might be?
:::
::::

Pathwise differentiability does not necessarily imply that there *is* a RAL estimator. It only allows one to exist. In the next part of this book we will study how to actually build efficient estimators and we will see that we need certain assumptions even to guarantee asymptotic linearity. Whether or not that can be done and in what context depends on estimand in question.

## Gradients

Tangent sets and pathwise derivatives are important tools that have already proven useful to us in characterizing when RAL estimators can even exist, but we can go further. In this section we'll build on these concepts to fully characterize all possible RAL estimators of any estimand in a pathwise differentiable model.

From here on out we will presume that the estimand is pathwise differentiable so that it is possible for the central identity $\dot\Psi_\p (s) = \p (s \phi)$ for all $s \in \tset_\p$ to hold for some function $\phi$. Our goal is to characterize the set of functions $\phi$ that can be influence functions, i.e. the set of functions that satisfy this identity. Once we know what all the possible options are for influence functions, we can easily compare them and choose the most "efficient" influence function to build an estimator around.

As previously discussed, if a function satisfies the identity it does not immediately mean that a real-world RAL estimator can be constructed, but we will say that it implies that RAL estimator exists "in principle". For that reason, we'll say that any function $\phi$ that satisfies the central identity is an influence function of a RAL estimator, even if such an estimator can't be built in practice without additional assumptions. We will deal with understanding those additional assumptions later.

::: callout-warning
At this point, understanding Riesz representation becomes important. I encourage you to read @sec-app-riesz and any other background material in @sec-app-L2 you need before proceeding. I promise you will find the material rewarding and immediately useful.
:::

All of this starts with pathwise differentiability. For a pathwise differentiable estimand, we know that $\dot\Psi$ is a bounded linear functional defined on the tangent set. In order to use an important result in functional analysis called the Riesz representation theorem we need to extend the pathwise derivative function $\dot\Psi$ so it is defined on an entire vector space. Although the tangent set is a vector space in all of the major examples we consider in this book, there are cases where it is not. I'll use the symbol $\tspace_\p$ to denote the linear closure of the tangent set, which I'll call the tangent *space*.

Often $\tset = \tspace$ already. A linear closure of a set of vectors is all possible linear combinations of those vectors along with any limits. Since it is linear and continuous, the pathwise derivative is easily defined on $\tspace_\p$. Any score function in this space is either a) a linear combination $\bar s = \sum c_j s_j$ of scores $s_j \in \tset_\p$, in which case we define $\dot\Psi (\bar s) = \sum c_j \dot\Psi(s)$ in accordance with linearity; or b) a limit of such combinations $\bar s = \lim_{n\to \infty} s_n$, in which case we define $\dot\Psi (\bar s) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \dot\Psi(s)$ in accordance with continuity. $\tspace_\p$ is always a subspace of $\eltwop$ and thus inherits its inner product $\langle f,g\rangle = \int fg \dd \p = \p fg$.

::: {#fig-tangent-space}

Cartoon of the relationship between the tangent set $\tset_\p$ and tangent space $\tspace_\p$. The tangent set is not always a subspace but it is always closed under positive scaling (prove it!), which is why it appears as a wedge in the cartoon. The tangent space fills in the rest of the plane that the tangent set sits in, i.e. it is the smallest subspace of $\eltwopz$ that contains the tangent set.
:::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-tangent-space}
For two models $\mathcal Q \subset \model$, what is the relationship between $\mathring{\mathcal Q}_\p$ and $\tspace_\p$ at any point $\p \in \mathcal Q$?
:::
::::

When the estimand is pathwise differentiable, the pathwise derivative $\dot\Psi$ is a bounded linear functional defined on the full tangent space $\tspace_\p$. Since it is bounded and linear, $\dot\Psi$ has some direction of steepest ascent and moreover the Riesz representation theorem formally guarantees that the application of $\dot\Psi$ to an argument $s$ is equivalent to taking the inner product of $s$ with some unique element of $\tspace_\p$ that points in that direction of steepest ascent. This is completely analogous to the way that the derivative in a direction $v \in \reals^d$ of a multivariable function $f(z)$ at $z_0$ can be computed by taking the dot product of that direction vector with the *gradient* of $f$ at $z_0$:

$$
\dot f_{z_0}(v) = \lim_{\eps \to 0} \frac{f(z_0 + \eps v) - f(z_0)}{\eps} = v \cdot \grad f.
$$

In $\reals^d$, the gradient vector $\grad f$ is precisely the Riesz representer of the directional derivative $\dot f$ (at $z_0$, but this is suppressed in the notation). For that reason, we'll use $\grad \Psi$ to denote the Riesz representer of the pathwise derivative $\dot \Psi_\p$ at $\p \in \model$ and call it the "gradient" of the estimand at that point. The direction of the Riesz representer corresponds to the direction of maximum slope for a linear functional. In the case of the pathwise derivative, this corresponds to the direction of maximum instantaneous rate of change of the estimand across paths with unit-norm scores.

:::: callout-note
# Gradient of a Pathwise Differentiable Estimand

::: {#def-gradient}
For an estimand $\Psi$ that is pathwise differentiable at $\p \in \model$, the *gradient* (or *canonical gradient*) $\grad_\p \Psi$ is the (unique) Riesz representer of the pathwise derivative $\dot\Psi: \tspace_\p \to \reals$.

The gradient is always an element of $\tspace_\p \subseteq \eltwopz$ and is thus square integrable and mean zero under $\p$ at a minimum.

The gradient represents the "direction" in which the estimand is increasing most quickly and its $\eltwop$ norm $\| \grad_\p \Psi \| = \dot\Psi(\frac{\grad_\p \Psi}{\|\grad_\p \Psi\|})$ encodes the speed at which it is instantaneously increasing in that direction.
:::
::::

For functions defined on $\reals^d$ the gradient is a familiar $d$-dimensional vector. The pathwise derivative is defined on the tangent space $\tspace_\p$, a subspace of the space of functions $\eltwopz$, and therefore the gradient of the estimand is also an $\eltwopz$ function: it must be square integrable and have mean zero under $\p$. The gradient depends on what point $\p$ the pathwise derivative is taken at and in what model $\model$, but these dependencies are often suppressed in the notation.

::: {#fig-gradient}
``` tikz

\def\PlaneHalfY{1}

\def\GradAngle{130} % in-plane gradient direction (deg)

% level-set controls

\resizebox{11cm}{!}{
\begin{tikzpicture}[tdplot_main_coords, scale=3.0, line cap=round, line join=round]

  % 3D axes
  \draw[->, thick] (0,0,0) -- (\AxisL,0,0);
  \draw[->, thick] (0,0,0) -- (0,\AxisL,0);
  \draw[->, thick] (0,0,0) -- (0,0,\AxisL);

  % rotated plane coords

  % === plane with transparent gradient, level sets, arrow ===
% === inside the rotated plane scope ===
\begin{scope}[tdplot_rotated_coords, canvas is xy plane at z=0]
  % gradient fill (transparent)

    \shade[shading=axis,
           left color=white, right color=blue,
           shading angle=\GradAngle]
      (-\PlaneHalfX,-\PlaneHalfY) rectangle (\PlaneHalfX,\PlaneHalfY);
  \end{scope}

  % border
  \draw[black, line width=0.4pt]
    (-\PlaneHalfX,-\PlaneHalfY) rectangle (\PlaneHalfX,\PlaneHalfY);

  % ----- level sets: perpendicular to gradient, full coverage -----
  \def\LevelSpacing{0.18}
  % half-projection length of the rectangle along the gradient direction
  \pgfmathsetmacro{\projHalf}{abs(cos(\GradAngle))*\PlaneHalfX + abs(sin(\GradAngle))*\PlaneHalfY}
  % long enough line segment (longer than plane diagonal)
  \pgfmathsetmacro{\LineHalfLen}{1.6*sqrt(\PlaneHalfX*\PlaneHalfX+\PlaneHalfY*\PlaneHalfY)}
  % integer count; +2 margin to be safe
  \pgfmathtruncatemacro{\N}{ceil( (2*\projHalf)/\LevelSpacing ) + 2}
  % starting offset so we cover both negative and positive sides evenly
  \pgfmathsetmacro{\start}{- \projHalf - \LevelSpacing}
  % directions
  \pgfmathsetmacro{\dx}{cos(\GradAngle+90)}
  \pgfmathsetmacro{\dy}{sin(\GradAngle+90)}

  \begin{scope}
    \clip (-\PlaneHalfX,-\PlaneHalfY) rectangle (\PlaneHalfX,\PlaneHalfY);
    \foreach \i in {0,...,\N}{
      \pgfmathsetmacro{\off}{\start + \i*\LevelSpacing}
      \draw[densely dotted, very thin, black, opacity=0.7]
        ({\off*cos(\GradAngle) - \LineHalfLen*\dx},
         {\off*sin(\GradAngle) - \LineHalfLen*\dy})
      --
        ({\off*cos(\GradAngle) + \LineHalfLen*\dx},
         {\off*sin(\GradAngle) + \LineHalfLen*\dy});
    }
  \end{scope}

  % label + arrow (unchanged)
  \node[black, anchor=south east] at (0, -0.9) {$\overset{\circ}{\mathcal P}$};
  \draw[->, blue, very thick]
    (0,0) -- ({0.85*\PlaneHalfX*cos(\GradAngle)},{0.85*\PlaneHalfX*sin(\GradAngle)});
  \node[anchor=west, blue]
    at ({0.85*\PlaneHalfX*cos(\GradAngle)},{0.85*\PlaneHalfX*sin(\GradAngle)}) {$\nabla\!\Psi$};
\end{scope}

  % === tiny legend OUTSIDE the plane scope, in figure coordinates ===
  % put it near the picture's bottom-right corner
% === legend in screen coords (no 3D projection) ===
\begin{scope}[tdplot_screen_coords]
  \path (current bounding box.south east) coordinate (SE);
  % place and size in cm for predictability
  \begin{scope}[shift={($(SE)+(-0.2,0)$)}, x=1cm, y=1cm]
    \def\LegendW{0.1}   % 2 cm wide
    \def\LegendH{0.6}   % 0.3 cm tall
    \shade[shading=axis, left color=blue, right color=white,
           shading angle=0] % 0 = left-to-right on the page
      (0,0) rectangle (\LegendW,\LegendH);
    \node[anchor=west] at (+0.1,0.5*\LegendH) {$\dot{\Psi}$};
  \end{scope}
\end{scope}

\end{tikzpicture}
}
```

Visual representation of the gradient. The value of the pathwise derivative function $\dot\Psi_\p$ is depicted on the domain $\tspace_\p$ using the blue shading: darker values indicate higher values of $\dot\Psi_\p(s)$ at each point $s \in \tspace_\p$. Thin dotted lines represent the level sets of the pathwise derivative. The gradient $\grad \Psi$ is shown as the dark blue arrow, representing the direction of fastest ascent of the linear function $\dot\Psi_\p$ and the speed of that ascent (spacing of the level sets; the closer together, the bigger the gradient). Since $\dot\Psi_\p$ is a derivative, larger values correspond to larger rates of increase of the estimand $\Psi$, meaning that the gradient corresponds to the direction of steepest instantaneous rate of increase of the estimand.
:::

The gradient is the Riesz representer of the pathwise derivative, so, by definition,

$$
\dot\Psi_\p (s) = \p s \grad \Psi \quad\text{for all } s \in \tspace_\p.
$$

This looks exactly like our central identity: $\dot\Psi_\p (s) = \p s \phi$ for all $s \in \tset_\p$. Since the gradient satisfies the identity for all scores in the tangent space, it certainly satisfies it for the subset of those that are in the tangent *set*. Therefore the gradient is an influence function for a RAL estimator! Since the gradient always exists (by Riesz representation), we have proven that every pathwise differentiable estimand has at least one RAL estimator. In fact, there may be many RAL estimators with this influence function, but by virtue of having the same influence function they are asymptotically equivalent.

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-gradient-norm}
Use the identity above to prove the claim in @def-gradient that $\| \grad_\p \Psi \| = \dot\Psi(\frac{\grad_\p \Psi}{\|\grad_\p \Psi\|})$.
:::
::::

::: {#exm-gradient-nonparam}
Let $\model$ be the set of all possible distributions of continuous random variables and presume the estimand of interest is the mean $\Psi(\p) = \E_\p[Z] = \int z p(z) \dd z$. Let $\psi_\p$ abbreviate the mean of $Z$ for a distribution $\p$. We'll see that the gradient for this estimand is easy to find in this model moreover that we can even construct an estimator that has the gradient as its influence function.

We have already shown that this model is locally nonparametric (see @exm-tangent-set-nonparam) so at any $\p$ the tangent set is $\tset_\p = \eltwopz$. For any bounded score $s \in \eltwopz$ we can construct the usual convex path $p_\eps = (1+ \eps s)p$ which has score $s$. For unbounded scores we could construct the more complicated paths described in @exm-tangent-set-nonparam but this adds complexity without adding understanding so we'll explain using the simpler convex paths.

For a convex path the pathwise derivative can be evaluated explicitly assuming enough regularity to pass the derivative through the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot\Psi(s) 
&= \left. \frac{\dd}{\dd \eps} \right|_{\eps=0} \Psi\big((1+\eps s)p\big) \\
&= \left. \frac{\dd}{\dd \eps} \right|_{\eps=0} \int z (1+\eps s(z)) p(z) \dd z \\
&= \int \left. \frac{\dd}{\dd \eps} \right|_{\eps=0} z (1+\eps s(z)) p(z) \dd z \\
&= \int  z s(z) p(z) \dd z 
\end{aligned}
$$

This last expression is exactly $\langle z \mapsto z, s \rangle_{\eltwop}$, i.e. an inner product with the score. We might be tempted to say that the gradient is $f(z) = z$ but this isn't right. The Riesz representer must be a function in the domain of the linear functional, which in this case is $\eltwopz$, zero-mean functions. But $f(z) = z$ is not zero-mean under $\p$, i.e. $\E_\p[f(Z)] = \psi_\p \ne 0$ in general, so this cannot be the gradient.

However, the situation is easily remedied. Any score $s$ is also mean-zero under $\p$, so

$$
0 = \int s(z) p(z) \dd z = \int \psi_\p s(z) p(z) \dd z,
$$

meaning that we can add this term to what we have above and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot\Psi(s) 
&= \int  z s(z) p(z) \dd z  + \underbrace{\int \psi_\p s(z) p(z) \dd z}_0
&= \int  (z - \psi_\p) s(z) p(z) \dd z.
\end{aligned}
$$

The function $z \mapsto z - \psi_\p$ *is* mean zero under $\p$ so it is in the tangent space. The equality above establishes that this is the gradient of the mean.

We saw in @exm-AL-sample-mean that $\phi(z) = z-\psi_\p$ is exactly the influence function of the sample mean $\hat\psi = \frac{1}{n} \sum Z_i$. We already know the sample mean is regular but the fact that its influence function satisfies @thm-RAL-IFs also proves that regularity.
:::

:::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
::: {#exr-gradient}
The gradient generally depends on the model, even though we hide this dependence in the notation. Fix the estimand $\Psi$ and a distribution $\p \in \mathcal Q \subset \model$. Let $\grad_{\p \in \mathcal Q}\Psi$ be the gradient in the smaller model and let $\grad_{\p \in \mathcal P}\Psi$ be the gradient in the larger model. Argue for why $\|\grad_{\p \in \mathcal Q}\Psi\| \le \|\grad_{\p \in \mathcal P}\Psi\|$. *Hint*: what is the relationship between the tangent spaces?
:::
::::

### Other Influence Functions

Using Riesz representation, we showed that for any pathwise differentiable estimand there is at least one function that can be the influence function of a RAL estimator (in principle). Now we will understand in what cases there can be RAL estimators with influence functions different than the gradient.

In general, Riesz representation says that the gradient is the *only* element $\phi$ in the tangent space for which $\dot\Psi (s) = \p s\phi$ for all scores in the tangent space. When the model is locally nonparametric at $\p$, that means the gradient is the only mean-zero, square-integrable function that satisfies that identity. But since any influence function must also be mean-zero and square integrable (@def-AL), that rules out the possibility that any other $\eltwopz$ function can be an influence function. Therefore in locally nonparametric models there is only *one* influence function (the gradient of the estimand) and thus all RAL estimators are asymptotically equivalent to each other.

By itself this fact is already incredibly useful since locally nonparametric models are among the most practical in the real world. We'll see in the next chapter that deriving the gradient (and thus the only influence function) in a nonparametric model is easy to do.

Things are more interesting when the model is not locally nonparametric, i.e. when the tangent space is *not* all of $\eltwopz$. Since the tangent space is a vector space, it has an orthogonal complement $\tspace_\p^\perp$ relative to $\eltwopz$. This is essentially the largest subspace of directions in which we are not allowed to pertrub the distribution $\p$ because doing so would take us out of the model. The elements of this space therefore cannot be scores at $\p \in \model$ but nonetheless they live with scores in the common space $\eltwopz$.

::: callout-warning
If need be, you should review @sec-app-l2-triangles and specifically @def-orth-sum to learn more about orthogonal complements in Hilbert spaces.
:::

By definition, any element $v \in \tspace^\perp$ is orthogonal to any score $s \in \tspace$. Some elements of the tangent *space* may not actually be scores but we'll refer to them as such anyways. Therefore $0 = \langle s, v \rangle_{\eltwop} = \p sv$ for *any* $s$. Starting with our influence function identity with $\phi = \grad \Psi$, we can therefore add $0=\p sv$ to the right-hand side without violating the equality:

$$
\dot\Psi_\p(s) = \p s (\grad \Psi + v) \quad\text{for all } s \in \tspace_\p.
$$

Moreover the functions $v$ in the orthogonal complement of the tangent space are the *only* functions for which this holds. This fact is formalized in @thm-RAL-IF-set and illustrated graphically in @fig-RAL-IF-set.

:::: callout-note
# Set of Influence Functions

::: {#thm-RAL-IF-set}
Any influence function of a RAL estimator of a pathwise differentiable estimand is an element of the set $\Phi_\p = \{\grad_\p\Psi + v: v\in \tspace_\p^\perp\}$ where $\tspace_\p^\perp$ is the orthogonal complement of the tangent space $\tspace_\p$ relative to $\eltwopz$. Any element of the set $\Phi$ is, in principle, the influence function of some RAL estimator.

In a locally nonparametric model, $\tspace_\p^\perp$ only contains the zero function so $\grad_\p\Psi$ is the only possible influence function of a RAL estimator.

As a corollary of @thm-RAL-IFs, any estimator that is asymptotically linear at $\p$ with an influence function in this set must be regular at $\p \in \model$.
:::
::::

::: {#fig-RAL-IF-set}
